claim: Simultaneous stimulation of the antennal lobes (ALs) and the ascending fibers of the ventral nerve cord (AFV) induces long-term enhancement (LTE) of subsequent AL-evoked MB responses.
source: Simultaneous stimulation of the antennal lobes (ALs) and the ascending fibers of the ventral nerve cord (AFV), two sensory inputs to the mushroom bodies (MBs), induces long-term enhancement (LTE) of subsequent AL-evoked MB responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: LTE induction requires activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs).
source: LTE induction requires activation of at least three signaling pathways to the MBs, mediated by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), NMDA receptors (NRs), and D1 dopamine receptors (D1Rs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a requirement for LTE induction.

claim: LTE induction requires activation of NMDA receptors (NRs).
source: LTE induction requires activation of at least three signaling pathways to the MBs, mediated by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), NMDA receptors (NRs), and D1 dopamine receptors (D1Rs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a requirement for LTE induction.

claim: LTE induction requires activation of D1 dopamine receptors (D1Rs).
source: LTE induction requires activation of at least three signaling pathways to the MBs, mediated by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), NMDA receptors (NRs), and D1 dopamine receptors (D1Rs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a requirement for LTE induction.

claim: Inputs from the AL are transmitted to the MBs through nAChRs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that inputs from the AL are transmitted to the MBs through nAChRs, and inputs from the AFV are transmitted by NRs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated finding.

claim: Inputs from the AFV are transmitted to the MBs by NRs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that inputs from the AL are transmitted to the MBs through nAChRs, and inputs from the AFV are transmitted by NRs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated finding.

claim: Dopamine signaling occurs downstream of both nAChR and NR activation.
source: Dopamine signaling occurs downstream of both nAChR and NR activation, and requires simultaneous stimulation of both pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated finding.

claim: Dopamine release requires simultaneous stimulation of both nAChR and NR pathways.
source: Dopamine signaling occurs downstream of both nAChR and NR activation, and requires simultaneous stimulation of both pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated finding.

claim: Dopamine release requires the activity of the rutabaga adenylyl cyclase in postsynaptic MB neurons.
source: Dopamine release requires the activity of the rutabaga adenylyl cyclase in postsynaptic MB neurons, and release is restricted to MB neurons that receive coincident stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated finding.

claim: Dopamine release is restricted to MB neurons that receive coincident stimulation.
source: Dopamine release requires the activity of the rutabaga adenylyl cyclase in postsynaptic MB neurons, and release is restricted to MB neurons that receive coincident stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a demonstrated finding.

claim: Postsynaptic activity can gate presynaptic dopamine release to regulate plasticity.
source: Our results indicate that postsynaptic activity can gate presynaptic dopamine release to regulate plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Dopamine (DA) signaling is required for associative learning and synaptic plasticity.
source: Dopamine (DA) signaling is required for associative learning and synaptic plasticity (Jay, 2003; Kim et al., 2007; Puig and Miller, 2012; Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In associative learning, DA activity often correlates with US presentation.
source: In associative learning, where a conditioned stimulus or CS (e.g. a neutral odor) is paired with an unconditioned stimulus or US (e.g. aversive electrical shocks or appetitive food rewards), DA activity often correlates with US presentation (Aso et al., 2010; Burke et al., 2012; Riemensperger et al., 2005; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Waddell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila, the activation of different subsets of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) can substitute for the presentation of aversive or appetitive stimuli during training.
source: Indeed, in Drosophila, the activation of different subsets of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) can substitute for the presentation of aversive or appetitive stimuli during training (Aso et al., 2010; Burke et al., 2012; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Waddell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DA functions to transmit US information to olfactory association areas in the Drosophila brain.
source: This suggests that DA functions to transmit US information to olfactory association areas in the Drosophila brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing DAN activation can substitute for US presentation.

claim: As animals learn to associate the CS with the US, DAN activity becomes correlated with the CS.
source: While the DAN activity initially correlates with US presentation, as animals learn to associate the CS with the US, activity becomes correlated with the CS (Wise, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work in mammals.

claim: DAN activity correlates with the unexpectedness of the US presentation.
source: DAN activity also correlates with the unexpectedness of the US presentation.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description of reward prediction error paradigms.

claim: In reward or punishment prediction error paradigms, an expected reward or punishment causes little change in DAN activity.
source: In reward or punishment prediction error paradigms, a reward or punishment that is expected causes little change in activity, while a reward or punishment that is obtained or withheld unexpectedly induces strong increases or decreases in activity (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Busto et al., 2010; Schultz, 2013; Waddell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In reward or punishment prediction error paradigms, an unexpected reward or punishment induces strong increases or decreases in DAN activity.
source: In reward or punishment prediction error paradigms, a reward or punishment that is expected causes little change in activity, while a reward or punishment that is obtained or withheld unexpectedly induces strong increases or decreases in activity (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Busto et al., 2010; Schultz, 2013; Waddell, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila aversive olfactory conditioning, presentation of a relatively neutral odor is paired with presentation of aversive electric shocks.
source: In Drosophila aversive olfactory conditioning, presentation of a relatively neutral odor is paired with presentation of aversive electric shocks (Quinn et al., 1974; Tully and Quinn, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work describing the conditioning paradigm.

claim: Flies learn to associate the odor with the aversive stimulus and subsequently avoid the odor.
source: Flies learn to associate the odor with the aversive stimulus and subsequently avoid the odor.
evidence: This is a well-established behavioral outcome of the conditioning paradigm.

claim: The odor-shock association forms in the mushroom bodies (MBs) of the Drosophila brain.
source: This association forms in the mushroom bodies (MBs) of the Drosophila brain (Heisenberg, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Odor information is transmitted to the MBs from the antennal lobes (ALs) via projection neurons.
source: Odor information is transmitted to the MBs from the antennal lobes (ALs) via projection neurons (Ito et al., 1998; Stocker, 1994), while shock information is likely transmitted from the body through the ascending fibers of the ventral nerve cord (AFV).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Shock information is likely transmitted from the body through the ascending fibers of the ventral nerve cord (AFV).
source: Odor information is transmitted to the MBs from the antennal lobes (ALs) via projection neurons (Ito et al., 1998; Stocker, 1994), while shock information is likely transmitted from the body through the ascending fibers of the ventral nerve cord (AFV).
evidence: This is stated as a likely pathway, suggesting it is an inference or hypothesis.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the ALs or AFV induces Ca2+ influx in the MBs of dissected brains.
source: Electrical stimulation of the ALs or AFV induces Ca2+ influx in the MBs of dissected brains.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors and others.

claim: Simultaneous stimulation of both the ALs and AFV causes long-term enhancement (LTE) of subsequent AL-induced Ca2+ responses in the MBs that lasts for at least two hours.
source: However, simultaneous stimulation of both the ALs and AFV causes long-term enhancement (LTE) of subsequent AL-induced Ca2+ responses in the MBs that lasts for at least two hours.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Both LTE and learning require activity of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs).
source: Both LTE and learning require activity of at least three neurotransmitter receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), NMDA receptors (NRs), and D1Rs (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Both LTE and learning require activity of NMDA receptors (NRs).
source: Both LTE and learning require activity of at least three neurotransmitter receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), NMDA receptors (NRs), and D1Rs (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Both LTE and learning require activity of D1Rs.
source: Both LTE and learning require activity of at least three neurotransmitter receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), NMDA receptors (NRs), and D1Rs (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: LTE formation requires associativity between the two input stimuli.
source: In addition, LTE formation requires associativity between the two input stimuli, since increasing the stimulus intensity or duration of one input is insufficient to bypass the requirement of the other (Ueno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Increasing the stimulus intensity or duration of one input is insufficient to bypass the requirement of the other input for LTE formation.
source: In addition, LTE formation requires associativity between the two input stimuli, since increasing the stimulus intensity or duration of one input is insufficient to bypass the requirement of the other (Ueno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: LTE displays input specificity, with MB responses to AL stimulation, but not AFV stimulation, being enhanced.
source: LTE also displays input specificity. MB responses to AL stimulation, but not AFV stimulation, are enhanced.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of LTE.

claim: During associative learning, responses to odors are modified, but not responses to electrical shocks.
source: Similarly, during associative learning, responses to odors are modified, but not responses to electrical shocks (Quinn et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LTE can be extinguished by repetitive AL stimulation in the absence of AFV stimulation.
source: Finally, LTE can be extinguished by repetitive AL stimulation in the absence of AFV stimulation (Ueno et al., 2013), a phenomenon reminiscent of learning extinction (Quinn et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AL stimulation causes synaptic vesicle exocytosis from PN terminals in the MB calyx.
source: Upon stimulation of the ALs, we observed increased spH fluorescence in PN terminals, including those in the MB calyx, the MB region receiving inputs from PNs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AL stimulation causes Ca2+ response in MB lobes.
source: We also observed robust Ca2+ responses in the vertical lobes of the MBs (Figure 1C), indicating that AL stimulation causes both synaptic vesicle exocytosis from PN terminals on the MB calyx and Ca2+ response in MB lobes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by R-GECO1 fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AFV stimulation does not evoke vesicular exocytosis from TH-DA neuron terminals.
source: When we next stimulated the AFV, we again observed robust Ca2+ responses in the MBs. However, we did not observe increased spH fluorescence in the MB vertical lobes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TH-DA neurons may not be directly responsible for transmitting AFV information to the MBs.
source: This suggests that, although DA signaling is required for LTE, TH-DA neurons may not be directly responsible for transmitting AFV information to the MBs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of spH fluorescence increase in TH-DA neurons upon AFV stimulation.

claim: The NR antagonist, MK801, impairs AFV-evoked MB Ca2+ responses.
source: We previously showed that the NR antagonist, MK801, impairs AFV-evoked MB Ca2+ responses and LTE (Ueno et al., 2013), suggesting that glutamate (Glu), rather than DA, may transmit AFV signals to the MBs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The NR antagonist, MK801, impairs LTE.
source: We previously showed that the NR antagonist, MK801, impairs AFV-evoked MB Ca2+ responses and LTE (Ueno et al., 2013), suggesting that glutamate (Glu), rather than DA, may transmit AFV signals to the MBs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Glutamate, rather than DA, may transmit AFV signals to the MBs.
source: We previously showed that the NR antagonist, MK801, impairs AFV-evoked MB Ca2+ responses and LTE (Ueno et al., 2013), suggesting that glutamate (Glu), rather than DA, may transmit AFV signals to the MBs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the effects of MK801.

claim: Synaptic terminals immunoreactive for the vesicular Glu transporter, VGLUT, have been identified at the tip of the MB vertical lobes.
source: Furthermore, synaptic terminals immunoreactive for the vesicular Glu transporter, VGLUT, have been identified at the tip of the MB vertical lobes, where LTE is strongly induced (Daniels et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LTE is strongly induced at the tip of the MB vertical lobes.
source: Furthermore, synaptic terminals immunoreactive for the vesicular Glu transporter, VGLUT, have been identified at the tip of the MB vertical lobes, where LTE is strongly induced (Daniels et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of LTE.

claim: AFV stimulation induces vesicular exocytosis from GMR51C07-VGlut terminals onto the MBs.
source: AFV stimulation caused significant increases in both spH and R-GECO1 fluorescence at the MB vertical lobe tips (Figure 1G), suggesting that stimulation induces exocytosis from GMR51C07-VGlut terminals onto the MBs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Inhibiting synaptic output from GMR51C07 neurons during learning impairs short-term memory when flies are trained at the restrictive temperature.
source: When GMR51C07>shits flies were trained in an aversive olfactory associative paradigm at the permissive temperature, short-term memory (STM) was unaffected compared to controls. In contrast, when these flies were trained at the restrictive temperature, memory was significantly impaired (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GMR51C07 cells release glutamate to the MBs upon AFV stimulation.
source: Thus, GMR51C07 cells both release glutamate to the MBs upon AFV stimulation, and are required during formation of aversive memories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spH imaging and behavioral experiments.

claim: GMR51C07 cells are required during formation of aversive memories.
source: Thus, GMR51C07 cells both release glutamate to the MBs upon AFV stimulation, and are required during formation of aversive memories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Nmdar1EP331 mutants are defective for AFV-induced MB Ca2+ responses.
source: Consistent with idea that Glu transmits AFV inputs required for LTE to the MBs, we found that a Drosophila NR1 hypomorphic mutant, Nmdar1EP331 (Xia et al., 2005), is defective for both AFV-induced MB Ca2+ responses (Figure 2A), and LTE (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ca2+ imaging shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nmdar1EP331 mutants are defective for LTE.
source: Consistent with idea that Glu transmits AFV inputs required for LTE to the MBs, we found that a Drosophila NR1 hypomorphic mutant, Nmdar1EP331 (Xia et al., 2005), is defective for both AFV-induced MB Ca2+ responses (Figure 2A), and LTE (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AFV stimulation can be replaced by the direct application of NMDA to induce LTE.
source: Furthermore, we found that AFV stimulation could be replaced by the direct application of NMDA by micropipette onto the terminals of the MB vertical lobes (Figure 2C), to induce LTE (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Application of NMDA in the absence of AL stimulation does not induce LTE.
source: Application of NMDA in the absence of AL stimulation did not induce LTE, indicating that NMDA can replace AFV, but not AL, stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements.

claim: Knocking down NRs in the MBs by expressing Nmdar2-IR from the OK107-GAL4 driver prevents AL+ NMDA-induced LTE.
source: To determine whether NRs in the MBs mediate NMDA signaling, we next knocked down NRs in the MBs by expressing inverted repeats of Nmdar2 (Nmdar2-IR) from the OK107-GAL4 driver, and found that coupled AL stimulation and NMDA application (AL+ NMDA) failed to induce LTE (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Knocking down NRs in the MBs inhibits learning (3 min memory) in adult Drosophila.
source: Knocking down NRs in the MBs also inhibited learning (3 min memory) in adult Drosophila, again suggesting a link between LTE and learning-associated plasticity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AFV input to the MBs is transmitted via Glu neurons onto MB NRs.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that AFV input to the MBs is transmitted via Glu neurons onto MB NRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: AL + NMDA-induced LTE is abolished in DopRf02676 null mutant brains.
source: To determine the epistatatic relationship between DA and Glu signaling during LTE induction, we examined AL + NMDA-induced LTE, and found that it is abolished in DopRf02676, DopR null mutant, brains (Kim et al., 2007) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of 50 μM of the Drosophila D1R antagonist, butaclamol, prevents induction of AL + NMDA-induced LTE in wild-type brains.
source: Furthermore, addition of 50 μM of the Drosophila D1R antagonist, butaclamol (Sugamori et al., 1995) prevented induction of AL + NMDA-induced LTE in wild-type brains (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: D1R functions downstream of Glu/NR signaling during LTE formation.
source: These results indicate that D1R functions downstream of Glu/NR signaling during LTE formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the epistasis experiments.

claim: AL stimulation paired with application of DA (AL + DA) induces significant LTE.
source: When AL stimulation was paired with application of DA (AL + DA), we observed significant LTE (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Application of DA alone in the absence of AL stimulation induces LTE.
source: Surprisingly, we also detected LTE formation upon application of DA alone in the absence of AL stimulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DA-induced LTE is not impaired in brains from Nmdar1EP331 mutants.
source: Further supporting this model, DA-induced LTE was not impaired in brains from Nmdar1EP331 mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DA-induced LTE is restored in DopRf02676 mutants by expressing a DopR transgene in the MBs.
source: The DA-induced LTE was fully restored in DopRf02676 mutants when DopR was expressed from c747-Gal4, a MB driver predominantly expressing GAL4 in α/β and γ lobes (Aso et al., 2009) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Dose response curves plotting LTE magnitude as a function of DA concentration are not different when DA is applied alone or with simultaneous AL stimulation.
source: Dose response curves plotting LTE magnitude as a function of DA concentration were not different when DA was applied alone or with simultaneous AL stimulation (Figure 3G), suggesting that the DA-induced LTE is unlikely to be an artifact of excess DA application.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response curves shown in Figure 3G.

claim: DA is required during LTE induction.
source: The addition of antagonist during DA treatment abolished LTE (Figure 4A), while addition during maintenance and expression phases had no effect (Figure 4B). This discounts the possibility that residual DA remaining after washout is a responsible expression or maintenance of LTE, and instead indicates that DA is required during LTE induction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: DA application induces LTE even under external Ca2+ free conditions.
source: DA application induced LTE even under external Ca2+ free conditions, and in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX), which prevents the generation of action potentials (Figure 4C), suggesting that DA release and MB D1R activation occur at a late step of LTE induction where subsequent neurotransmission is not required.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DA application induces LTE in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: DA application induced LTE even under external Ca2+ free conditions, and in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX), which prevents the generation of action potentials (Figure 4C), suggesting that DA release and MB D1R activation occur at a late step of LTE induction where subsequent neurotransmission is not required.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DA release and MB D1R activation occur at a late step of LTE induction where subsequent neurotransmission is not required.
source: DA application induced LTE even under external Ca2+ free conditions, and in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX), which prevents the generation of action potentials (Figure 4C), suggesting that DA release and MB D1R activation occur at a late step of LTE induction where subsequent neurotransmission is not required.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TTX and Ca2+ free experiments.

claim: Simultaneous AL stimulation and NMDA application induces significant elevation of spH fluorescence from TH-DA neuron terminals on the MB vertical lobes.
source: To test this, we re-examined vesicular exocytosis from TH-DA neuron terminals by expressing spH in TH-DA neurons, and observed significant elevation of spH fluorescence from TH-DA neuron terminals on the MB vertical lobes upon simultaneous AL stimulation and NMDA application (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: spH fluorescence is unchanged in TH-DA neuron terminals upon either AL stimulation or NMDA application alone.
source: spH fluorescence was unchanged upon either AL stimulation or NMDA application alone.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the spH imaging experiments.

claim: Simultaneous AL and AFV stimulation induces significant increase in spH fluorescence in TH-DA neuron terminals.
source: Likewise, spH fluorescence increased significantly in TH-DA neuron terminals upon simultaneous AL and AFV stimulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Presynaptic DA release is gated by postsynaptic MB neurons that are activated by coincident AL and AFV inputs.
source: These results are consistent with a model where presynaptic DA release is gated by postsynaptic MB neurons that are activated by coincident AL and AFV inputs.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental results.

claim: Expression of nAChRα7Y195T in MBs disrupts cholinergic transmission from AL to MBs.
source: We confirmed that the expression of nAChRα7Y195T in MBs effectively disrupts both cholinergic transmission from AL to MBs and release of DA from TH-DA terminals upon AL + NMDA stimulation (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Expression of nAChRα7Y195T in MBs disrupts release of DA from TH-DA terminals upon AL + NMDA stimulation.
source: We confirmed that the expression of nAChRα7Y195T in MBs effectively disrupts both cholinergic transmission from AL to MBs and release of DA from TH-DA terminals upon AL + NMDA stimulation (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Expression of nAChRα7Y195T in TH-DA neurons does not prevent DA release upon coincident AL + NMDA stimulation.
source: However, when we expressed nAChRα7Y195T in TH-DA neurons, we still observed significant increases in spH fluorescence from TH-DA neuron terminals upon coincident AL + NMDA stimulation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Coincident inputs to MBs, but not TH-DA neurons, are required for DA release.
source: This suggests that coincident inputs to MBs, but not TH-DA neurons, are required for DA release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the nAChR dominant negative experiments.

claim: Rut-AC is required for LTE formation.
source: We next examined the mechanism through which MB neurons might detect coincident inputs. In Drosophila, the rutabaga (rut) gene encodes an adenylyl cyclase (Rut-AC) that is required in the MBs during associative learning (Busto et al., 2010), and is proposed to function as a coincidence detector. We found that Rut-AC is also required for LTE formation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTE measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: DA release following coincident AL + NMDA stimulation is significantly impaired in rut2080 mutants.
source: To determine whether Rut-AC is required for DA release following coincident AL + NMDA stimulation, we examined release in rut2080 mutants (Levin et al., 1992), and observed significant impairments (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figures 6B and 6D.

claim: DA release is restored when a rut transgene is re-expressed in the MBs from the 30Y-GAL4 MB driver in rut2080 mutants.
source: Significantly release was restored when a rut transgene (rut+) was re-expressed in the MBs from the 30Y-GAL4 MB driver (Figure 6C and D), indicating that the presynaptic DA vesicle release is regulated by post-synaptic MB neurons through a Rut-AC-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Presynaptic DA vesicle release is regulated by post-synaptic MB neurons through a Rut-AC-dependent mechanism.
source: Significantly release was restored when a rut transgene (rut+) was re-expressed in the MBs from the 30Y-GAL4 MB driver (Figure 6C and D), indicating that the presynaptic DA vesicle release is regulated by post-synaptic MB neurons through a Rut-AC-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: Most TH-DA neurons project their terminals bilaterally onto the MBs in both hemispheres of the brain.
source: Previous work has shown that most TH-DA neurons project their terminals bilaterally onto the MBs in both hemispheres of the brain (Mao and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PNs connect the ALs only to ipsilateral MBs.
source: The ALs are bilateral structures, and anatomical and physiological studies show that PNs connect the ALs only to ipsilateral MBs (Marin et al., 2002; Ueno et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Simultaneous AL + NMDA stimulation induces DA release only on the MB lobes ipsilateral to AL stimulation.
source: We monitored vesicular exocytosis from TH-DA neuronal terminals in response to simultaneous AL + NMDA stimulation (Figure 7A), and observed DA release only on the MB lobes ipsilateral to AL stimulation (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spH fluorescence imaging shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Postsynaptic gating mechanisms are able to restrict the location of DA release, even though DA neurons innervate extensive brain areas.
source: Thus, postsynaptic gating mechanisms are able to restrict the location of DA release, even though DA neurons innervate extensive brain areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unilateral DA release experiments.

claim: For LTE in the MBs, DA is unlikely to transmit sensory information, but instead plays a critical mechanistic role in LTE establishment at a step after sensory input.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that for LTE in the MBs, DA is unlikely to transmit sensory information, but instead, plays a critical mechanistic role in LTE establishment at a step after sensory input.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: DA is not released by activation of individual sensory inputs.
source: DA is not released by activation of individual sensory inputs, but instead requires coincident stimulation, indicating that DA functions downstream of a coincidence detector.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: DA requires coincident stimulation for release.
source: DA is not released by activation of individual sensory inputs, but instead requires coincident stimulation, indicating that DA functions downstream of a coincidence detector.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: DA functions downstream of a coincidence detector.
source: DA is not released by activation of individual sensory inputs, but instead requires coincident stimulation, indicating that DA functions downstream of a coincidence detector.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the requirement for coincident stimulation.

claim: Blocking DA signaling abolishes LTE.
source: Blocking DA signaling abolishes LTE, while DA release alone is sufficient to induce LTE, demonstrating the essential nature of DA in LTE formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: DA release alone is sufficient to induce LTE.
source: Blocking DA signaling abolishes LTE, while DA release alone is sufficient to induce LTE, demonstrating the essential nature of DA in LTE formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: LTE is likely related to learning and memory-associated plastic changes.
source: Although LTE is a phenomenon observed in vitro, we propose that it is likely related to learning and memory-associated plastic changes.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the similarities between LTE and learning.

claim: Aversive olfactory learning involves associations between odor information transmitted to the MBs via PNs from the antennal lobes, and shock information likely transmitted to the brain via the AFV.
source: Aversive olfactory learning involves associations between odor information, which is transmitted to the MBs via PNs from the antennal lobes, and shock information, which is likely transmitted to the brain via the AFV.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and the authors' findings.

claim: Both LTE and learning (3 min memory) require the activity of NRs in the MBs.
source: In the current manuscript, we further demonstrate that both LTE and learning (3 min memory) require the activity of NRs in the MBs, and identify a subset of glutamatergic neurons (using the GMR51C07 line), which are required for memory, and exhibit vesicular exocytosis onto MB vertical lobes upon AFV stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: A subset of glutamatergic neurons (using the GMR51C07 line) are required for memory.
source: In the current manuscript, we further demonstrate that both LTE and learning (3 min memory) require the activity of NRs in the MBs, and identify a subset of glutamatergic neurons (using the GMR51C07 line), which are required for memory, and exhibit vesicular exocytosis onto MB vertical lobes upon AFV stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: GMR51C07 glutamatergic neurons exhibit vesicular exocytosis onto MB vertical lobes upon AFV stimulation.
source: In the current manuscript, we further demonstrate that both LTE and learning (3 min memory) require the activity of NRs in the MBs, and identify a subset of glutamatergic neurons (using the GMR51C07 line), which are required for memory, and exhibit vesicular exocytosis onto MB vertical lobes upon AFV stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: AL stimulation evokes vesicular exocytosis from cholinergic PN terminals in the MB calyx.
source: Our synapto-pHluorin data indicate that AL stimulation evokes vesicular exocytosis from cholinergic PN terminals in the MB calyx, a result consistent with previous studies (Heisenberg, 2003; Su and O'Dowd, 2003; Yasuyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spH imaging data and is consistent with prior work.

claim: AFV stimulation evokes exocytosis from glutamatergic neurons rather than DANs.
source: However, we find that AFV stimulation evokes exocytosis from glutamatergic neurons rather than DANs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spH imaging data.

claim: Direct application of NMDA to the MBs can replace AFV stimulation during LTE induction.
source: Significantly, direct application of NMDA to the MBs can replace AFV stimulation during LTE induction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: NMDA acts through NRs in the MBs to induce LTE.
source: NMDA acts through NRs in the MBs to induce LTE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The final step in transmission of US information from the AFV to the MBs occurs through glutamatergic neurons activating MB NRs.
source: Thus, although the complete neural pathway from the AFV to the MBs has not yet been identified, our results suggest that the final step in transmission of US information from the AFV to the MBs occurs through glutamatergic neurons activating MB NRs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: DA release occurs at a step after cholinergic and glutamatergic activation of the MBs.
source: DA release occurs at a step after cholinergic and glutamatergic activation of the MBs, since LTE induced by AL + NMDA stimulation requires D1Rs, while LTE induced by the DA application does not require NR activity or AL stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the epistasis experiments.

claim: DA release and activation of D1Rs in the MBs comprise the last intercellular step during LTE establishment.
source: Furthermore, DA application induces LTE even in the presence of TTX in Ca2+ free media, suggesting that DA release and activation of D1Rs in the MBs comprise the last intercellular step during LTE establishment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TTX and Ca2+ free experiments.

claim: Exogenous activation of dopaminergic pathways can induce plasticity in MB Kenyon cell to MB output neuron transmission in Drosophila.
source: Similar to DA-induced plasticity in AL-MB transmission, previous papers have also found that exogenous activation of dopaminergic pathways can induce plasticity in MB Kenyon cell to MB output neuron transmission in Drosophila (Cohn et al., 2015), and in CA3 to CA1 transmission in rats and guinea pigs (Huang and Kandel, 1995; Williams et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Exogenous activation of dopaminergic pathways can induce plasticity in CA3 to CA1 transmission in rats and guinea pigs.
source: Similar to DA-induced plasticity in AL-MB transmission, previous papers have also found that exogenous activation of dopaminergic pathways can induce plasticity in MB Kenyon cell to MB output neuron transmission in Drosophila (Cohn et al., 2015), and in CA3 to CA1 transmission in rats and guinea pigs (Huang and Kandel, 1995; Williams et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rut-AC is proposed to function as a coincidence detector of olfactory and somatosensory inputs during olfactory learning.
source: Rut-AC is proposed to function as a coincidence detector of olfactory and somatosensory inputs during olfactory learning (Boto et al., 2014; Busto et al., 2010; Heisenberg, 2003; Tomchik and Davis, 2009), suggesting that coincident AL and AFV-mediated activation of postsynaptic Kenyon cells functions to gate presynaptic dopaminergic release through a Rut-AC-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Coincident AL and AFV-mediated activation of postsynaptic Kenyon cells functions to gate presynaptic dopaminergic release through a Rut-AC-dependent mechanism.
source: Rut-AC is proposed to function as a coincidence detector of olfactory and somatosensory inputs during olfactory learning (Boto et al., 2014; Busto et al., 2010; Heisenberg, 2003; Tomchik and Davis, 2009), suggesting that coincident AL and AFV-mediated activation of postsynaptic Kenyon cells functions to gate presynaptic dopaminergic release through a Rut-AC-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and prior work.

claim: Simultaneous AL and AFV inputs specify the appropriate targets where DA needs to be released.
source: Thus, simultaneous AL and AFV inputs specify the appropriate targets where DA needs to be released, while the amount of released DA may regulate the occurrence and intensity of plastic changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The amount of released DA may regulate the occurrence and intensity of plastic changes.
source: Thus, simultaneous AL and AFV inputs specify the appropriate targets where DA needs to be released, while the amount of released DA may regulate the occurrence and intensity of plastic changes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Rut-AC is activated by both Ca2+/calmodulin and G-protein-mediated signaling.
source: Previous studies have shown that Rut-AC is activated by both Ca2+/calmodulin and G-protein-mediated signaling, and may function to integrate these two signaling pathways (Levin et al., 1992; Tomchik and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rut-AC may function to integrate Ca2+/calmodulin and G-protein-mediated signaling pathways.
source: Previous studies have shown that Rut-AC is activated by both Ca2+/calmodulin and G-protein-mediated signaling, and may function to integrate these two signaling pathways (Levin et al., 1992; Tomchik and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The activation of neuronal gene expression by L-type voltage gated Ca2+ channels requires two independent activation mechanisms: Ca2+ influx, and a separate voltage-dependent conformational change.
source: Alternatively, Tsien and colleagues have recently demonstrated that the activation of neuronal gene expression by L-type voltage gated Ca2+ channels requires two independent activation mechanisms: Ca2+ influx, and a separate voltage-dependent conformational change (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neither Ca2+ influx nor voltage-dependent conformational change alone is sufficient for activation of neuronal gene expression by L-type voltage gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Neither signal alone is sufficient for activation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited work.

claim: Rut-AC, or another coincidence detector in the MBs may require convergent activation by Ca2+ influx from NRs, and a conformational change induced by action potentials propagated from the calyx.
source: Similarly, Rut-AC, or another coincidence detector in the MBs may require convergent activation by Ca2+ influx from NRs, and a conformational change induced by action potentials propagated from the calyx.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the analogy to L-type Ca2+ channels.

claim: Formation and storage of short-term memories (STMs) require γ and α'/β' Kenyon cells.
source: In Drosophila, formation and storage of short-term memories (STMs) require γ and α'/β' Kenyon cells, while consolidation to long-term memories (LTMs) is proposed to require α/β Kenyon cells (Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014; Krashes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Consolidation to long-term memories (LTMs) is proposed to require α/β Kenyon cells.
source: In Drosophila, formation and storage of short-term memories (STMs) require γ and α'/β' Kenyon cells, while consolidation to long-term memories (LTMs) is proposed to require α/β Kenyon cells (Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014; Krashes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LTE occurs in both the α and α' lobes.
source: In our study, we measured LTE at the vertical lobes, and previously demonstrated that LTE occurs in both the α and α' lobes (Ueno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: LTE may be associated with both STM and LTM.
source: Thus LTE may be associated with both STM and LTM.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the location of LTE and the memory requirements of different Kenyon cell types.

claim: Rutabaga expression in α/β neurons is necessary for LTM, but not STM.
source: Consistent with a role of LTE in LTM, a previous study by Blum et al. reported that rutabaga expression in α/β neurons is necessary for LTM, but not STM (Blum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NRs are required for LTM in the ellipsoid bodies.
source: Although NRs are also required LTM, this requirement is in the ellipsoid bodies, a brain region distinct from the MBs (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LTE may be important for both STM and LTM.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that LTE may be important for both STM and LTM, and may be a general mechanism for DA-mediated plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and prior work.

claim: LTE may be a general mechanism for DA-mediated plasticity.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that LTE may be important for both STM and LTM, and may be a general mechanism for DA-mediated plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Artificial activation of DANs can replace US exposure during learning.
source: Finally, we note that our results show an apparent discrepancy with previous work demonstrating that artificial activation of DANs can replace US exposure during learning (Aso et al., 2010; Burke et al., 2012; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Incorporating a dopaminergic feedback loop may allow the organism to fine tune the amount of learning that occurs based on factors including the physiological state of the organism.
source: Incorporating a dopaminergic feedback loop may allow the organism to fine tune the amount of learning that occurs based factors including the physiological state of the organism.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the dopaminergic feedback loop.
